citation: Dalgarno, Barney, & Mark J. W. Lee. (2012). Exploring the relationship between afforded learning tasks and learning benefits in 3D virtual learning environments. In Future Challenges, Sustainable Futures: Proceedings ascilite Wellington 2012 (pp. 236–245). ****** UNVERIFIED note: this paper's own reference list cites its parent model as 'Dalgarno, B. & Lee, M.J.W. (2010). ... British Journal of Educational Technology, 40(6), 10-32' — both year (2010 vs. this cluster's ped-sec-04 manifest year of 2009) and volume (40(6) vs. ped-sec-04's citation of 41(1)) diverge; flagged per plan instruction, not resolved.
thesis: Returning to their own 2009/2010 affordances-of-3D-VLEs model, Dalgarno and Lee survey 53 of 117 higher-education respondents on which of the model's five hypothesized learning benefits they perceived occurring, and test via MANOVA whether ten grounded-coded categories of afforded learning task predict specific benefit ratings; results show strong, near-uniform endorsement of all five benefits regardless of activity type, with significant activity-category effects for only two of five benefits (place/object familiarity; motivation/engagement, both driven by the 'instruction' category) — a self-authored empirical qualification of the parent model's task-to-benefit specificity, attributed tentatively to multi-category task confounding and/or enthusiast-respondent positive bias.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.summary: States the paper extends the authors' own 2010 3D-VLE affordances model by relating afforded learning tasks to reported learning benefits using survey data from 53 of 117 HE respondents; results strongly support all five benefits occurring but leave task-to-benefit links unclear (p.236).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Recaps the BJET model (cited as 'Dalgarno & Lee, 2010'): 10 distinguishing characteristics, 3 intermediate experiential outcomes (identity, presence, co-presence), 5 learning benefits; states this paper's two aims — gauge perceived benefit strength; explore task-to-benefit relationship (p.236).

sections.title: Background and related work
sections.summary: Surveys prior 3D-VLE/Second Life activity taxonomies (Ryan; Kay & FitzGerald; Jiang; Hew & Cheung) and affordance accounts (Hollins & Robbins; Warburton & Pérez García; Lim; Dickey); adopts Norman's (1999) real-vs-perceived affordance distinction; notes most prior sources conflate affordances with benefits (pp.236-238).

sections.title: Methods and data sources
sections.summary: Part of a DEHub-funded Australia/New Zealand scoping study (N=117 HE academic staff); this paper analyzes the 53 who described detailed 3D-VLE use. Q116 (open-ended activity description) grounded-coded via Corbin & Strauss (2008) constant-comparison method; Q120 (five 7-point-Likert benefit items) (p.238-239).

sections.title: Results — categories of learning activity
sections.summary: Ten non-exclusive grounded categories emerged: place exploration, concept exploration, task practice, role-play, gaming, communication, slide show, building/scripting, instruction, machinima, plus 'Other' and one uncoded response (pp.239-240).

sections.title: Results — reported learning benefits
sections.summary: Table 1: high mean agreement (5.0-5.9, N=53) across all five benefit statements; most respondents endorsed every benefit regardless of activity design (p.241).

sections.title: Results — comparing learning activities to reported benefits
sections.summary: MANOVA (11 activity categories x 5 benefit DVs) found significant main effects for only 2 of 5 benefits: place/object familiarity (F(1,40)=4.841, p=.034) and motivation/engagement (F(1,40)=4.136, p=.049), both driven by the 'instruction' category scoring higher; none of the authors' a priori hypothesized links reached significance (pp.241-243).

sections.title: Discussion and recommendations for future research
sections.summary: Proposes two explanations for the largely null MANOVA results: multi-category task confounding, and enthusiast self-selection/positive-attitude bias among respondents. Recommends controlled comparisons (flagging Clark 1994's media-vs-method confound and ethical access issues), student- (not just educator-) perceived benefit data, and attention to Norman's perceived-affordance gap between students and educators (pp.243-244).

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Restates that task-to-benefit links remain empirically unclear despite strong overall benefit endorsement; calls for future work combining student-perceived-affordance data with assessment of actual learning outcomes (pp.244-245).

constructs.label: representational fidelity
constructs.treatment: operationalized via Q120(a) 'assisted learners in developing familiarity with a place and the objects within it' (M=5.0, N=53), testing ped-sec-04's Affordance 1 (spatial knowledge representation)

constructs.label: affect: enjoyment & intrinsic motivation
constructs.treatment: operationalized via Q120(b) 'was motivating and engaging for learners' (M=5.9, the single highest-rated benefit), testing ped-sec-04's Affordance 3

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: same Q120(b) item; the only benefit besides familiarity to show a significant MANOVA activity-category effect (F(1,40)=4.136, p=.049, instruction category)

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: operationalized via Q120(c) 'led to improved transfer of learning to real situations' (M=5.5), testing ped-sec-04's Affordance 4

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: operationalized via Q120(d) 'led to more effective collaborative learning' (M=5.6), testing ped-sec-04's Affordance 5; no significant MANOVA effect found for the hypothesized 'communication' activity-category link

constructs.label: learning outcomes: procedural / skills
constructs.treatment: operationalized via Q120(e) 'allowed learners to learn through experience in context' (M=5.8), testing ped-sec-04's Affordance 2 (experiential tasks)

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.design: questionnaire survey (N=117, analytic subsample N=53) of HE academic staff describing 3D-VLE (chiefly Second Life-type multi-user world) use with their students; part of the DEHub Australia/New Zealand scoping study (Dalgarno et al. 2011a); grounded-coded open-ended activity description (Q116, Corbin & Strauss 2008 constant-comparison method) x 7-point Likert benefit ratings (Q120); MANOVA (11 activity categories IV x 5 benefit ratings DV)

readings.claim: Respondents strongly endorsed all five hypothesized learning benefits essentially regardless of activity/task type undertaken.

MANOVA found a significant activity-category main effect for only two of five benefits (place/object familiarity; motivation/engagement), both driven by the 'instruction' category scoring higher; none of the authors' a priori hypothesized task-benefit links reached significance.

The largely null MANOVA result may reflect either multi-category task confounding (most activities spanned more than one coded category) or enthusiast self-selection/positive-attitude bias among respondents rather than genuine evidence-based benefit differentiation.
Controlled 3D-VLE-vs-non-3D-VLE comparison studies are confounded by media-vs-method issues (after Clark, 1994) and raise access-ethics problems in authentic university contexts.
Future research should collect student- rather than solely educator-perceived benefit data, and attend to the perceived-affordance gap (Norman, 1999) between students and educators.

tensions.axis: the parent model's optimistic five-affordance structure vs. this follow-up's largely null task-to-benefit MANOVA result
tensions.note: The same authorial team's own empirical test finds strong benefit endorsement but almost no activity-category specificity, weakening (without abandoning) confidence in the fine-grained task-to-benefit links their 2009/2010 model proposes; the authors themselves offer a self-critical enthusiast-bias explanation rather than declaring the model disconfirmed.

tensions.axis: educator-perceived benefit (this study's data) vs. student-perceived benefit (explicitly not collected here)
tensions.note: The authors flag this as their own study's central limitation: educator enthusiasm/investment may inflate benefit ratings relative to what students themselves would report, per Norman's perceived-affordance framework.
